newsitem.title: UK: Party row for Blair at first byelection as premier.
newsitem.headline: Party row for Blair at first byelection as premier.

text.p: Tony Blair's triumphant post-election progress hit a pothole on Friday as a row escalated over the choice of Labour's parliamentary candidate for the first by-election of the new government.

The prime minister, who won a 179-seat majority at Britain's May 1 general election, went to Uxbridge, west London, to support Labour's Andrew Slaughter ahead of the vote on July 31 when the ruling party hopes to take the seat from the Conservatives.
But even before he arrived, Slaughter's Conservative opponents were crowing over the defection of a local Labour activist and former parliamentary candidate, Michael Shrimpton.
Shrimpton said he was joining the Conservatives partly because of the party's decision to dump its general election standard-bearer, David Williams, in favour of Slaughter.
"I'd always assumed that David Williams would get it. The fact that he wasn't even shortlisted astonished me," Shrimpton told BBC radio.
"There is deep concern within the Labour Party...at the way the party machine is becoming centralised and overriding the wishes of local constituency activists."

The move had already prompted a long-serving councillor, Brian Hudson, to resign from the local Labour group on the local Hillingdon Council, and there have been reports that up to 30 local Labour activists have refused to campaign for Slaughter.
Blair has been accused by many Labour supporters of centralising power in a small clique of advisers which decides policy with little discussion with outsiders, even parliamentary colleagues.
Blair ignored the row as he arrived in Uxbridge, defying accepted convention that prime ministers do not campaign in parliamentary by-elections.
Instead he made a speech promising "not just over the next couple of months but the next few years...to deliver to people the type of Britain we want to see".
But one bystander shouted after him: "Why haven't you picked the local man?"

The by-election was caused by the death of Sir Michael Shersby, who retained the commuter town seat for the Conservatives in May, but saw his 13,179 vote majority shrivel to just 724. The Conservatives had been in power nationally since 1979.

A victory for Labour in Uxbridge would signal that Blair's "honeymoon period" with British voters was not over. It is extremely rare for a ruling party to gain a seat, however marginal, from the opposition at a by-election.
The Conservative candidate is John Randall, a local shopkeeper with impeccable Uxbridge roots, and Shersby's election agent in May.
The previous government had not even retained a Conservative seat since a by-election in rural Yorkshire in February 1989.
Ironically, the victor at that Richmond contest, with a reduced majority, was William Hague, the man chosen last month to succeed beaten prime minister John Major as Conservative Party leader.
